title: The quickest slide down to a point off to one side isn’t a straight line but a cycloid

cover.alt: A computer rendering of five curved blue tracks running side by side down to a common wall, with coloured balls at different points along them.

body: Picture a bead sliding without friction from one point to a lower point off to the side. The straight line is the shortest path, but not the quickest: a track that drops steeply at first lets the bead build up speed early. The best trade-off, the **brachistochrone** (Greek for “shortest time”), is a cycloid, the curve traced by a point on the rim of a rolling wheel. Johann Bernoulli set the problem as a challenge in 1696, and Isaac Newton, Jakob Bernoulli, Leibniz, Tschirnhaus and L’Hôpital all sent in solutions.

slides.alt: Computer animation at half speed: five identical balls start at the same height on five differently curved frictionless tracks and roll down to a wall. The yellow ball on the second track arrives first; the red ball, on the track that drops steepest at the start, comes fourth.
slides.caption: Half speed: five identical balls race down five frictionless tracks. Yellow, on the cycloid, wins. Red drops steepest at the start but only comes fourth.
slides.credit: PantheraLeo1359531 · CC0 · excerpt, slowed to half speed

left.label: Galileo, 1638
left.text: The quickest way down is along an arc of a circle.

right.label: The answer, 1697
right.text: It is a cycloid, the curve a point on a rolling wheel’s rim traces out.

events.text: Galileo concludes the fastest path is a circular arc
Johann Bernoulli sets the problem in the journal Acta Eruditorum
Newton reportedly solves it in one night and mails it anonymously

slides.heading: Known by his claw
slides.text: Newton’s answer arrived without a name, but Johann Bernoulli is said to have known at once who wrote it, as you recognise a lion from its claw mark. The famous Latin version of the line, “tanquam ex ungue leonem”, comes from an 1855 biography of Newton.

slides.question: Would a much heavier ball need a different fastest curve?
slides.explanation: The fastest curve, the brachistochrone, doesn’t depend on the ball’s mass or on the strength of gravity. Stronger gravity makes every ball faster, but the same curve still wins.
